pac_metadata.title: Viking Age Scandinavia
pac_metadata.description: This PAC focuses on Viking Age Scandinavia during the peak of Viking activity in England, from the arrival of the Great Heathen Army to the end of Norse influence after the Battle of Hastings. It covers the cultural context of the raiders, traders, and settlers originating from Scandinavia.

dwellings.description: Mainly longhouses, accommodating families, livestock, and storage. Sizes varied based on wealth and status.
key_features: Rectangular shape with rounded corners
Long central hearth for heating and cooking
Internal timber posts supporting the roof
Divided internal space (living area, animal stalls, storage)
Often turf or thatch roofs
Walls of wattle-and-daub or horizontal timbers

public_structures.description: Gathering places for legal assemblies, trade, and religious worship.
key_features: Thing sites (outdoor assembly places, often marked by stones or mounds)
Market towns (Kaupangr, Emporia) with workshops, stalls, and jetties
Feasting halls (potentially separate large buildings or larger longhouses)

religious_structures.description: Sites dedicated to the worship of the Norse gods. Evidence suggests varied forms.
key_features: Open-air cult sites (hörgr) with altars (stalli) or sacred trees/groves
Temple buildings (hofs) - archaeological evidence is scarce, suggesting timber halls adapted for ritual use or specific structures with inner sanctuaries
Image houses for idols (statuettes)

construction_techniques.description: Based on local materials, primarily wood.
key_features: Post-and-plank construction
Stave construction (for later churches, perhaps influenced religious buildings)
Wattle-and-daub walls
Turf or thatch roofing over timber frames
Stone foundations or sleeper beams

everyday_male.description: Layered clothing for warmth, practical for physical labor and travel.
items: Trousers (brók) varying from loose to fitted, often tied or belted
Leg wraps or hose for lower legs
Cloak (kápa or feldr) fastened with a brooch
Belt (leðrgyrðill) for carrying pouches or tools

ceremonial_male.description: Similar layers but made from finer materials, brighter colors, and adorned with jewelry or embroidery.
items: Brooches (e.g., penannular) of silver or bronze, sometimes gold
Imported fabrics like silk or brocade (for wealthy)

everyday_female.description: Layered dresses, often with an outer garment supported by brooches.
items: Hangerock or Overdress (smokkr or pinafore dress) suspended by straps over the shoulders, fastened with two large brooches (tortoise brooches)
Woolen gown (kyrtill) worn as an outer layer or alternative to hangerock
Shawl or cloak fastened with a brooch

ceremonial_female.description: Finer fabrics, more elaborate embroidery, and significant jewelry.
items: Dresses from better quality wool, linen, or imported fabrics (silk)
Pairs of decorative tortoise brooches (often connected by chains with pendants, beads, or tools)
Third brooch (often trefoil or round) fastening a shawl or neckline
Necklaces (beads of glass, amber, silver, gold)

materials: Bronze, Silver, Gold (for jewelry and fittings)
colors: Red, Blue, Yellow, Green, Brown, Grey, White (natural wool/linen colors)
decorative_elements: Metal fittings on belts and straps

status_indicators_clothing.description: Status was indicated by the quality of fabric, brightness/rarity of colors, amount and material of jewelry, and presence of imported goods.

weapons.description: Essential tools for raiding, warfare, and personal defense.
types: Swords (single or double-edged, pattern-welded blades highly prized)
Axes (battle axes, including the large 'Danish axe', and smaller throwing axes)
Bows and Arrows (wood bows, iron arrowheads)
Knives (seax - large fighting knife, and smaller utility knives)

armor.description: Protection varied by status; mail shirts were expensive.
types: Round shields (wood with a central iron boss)
Helmets (typically simple iron caps or segmented helmets, NO horns)
Mail shirts (byrnja - made of interlinked rings, expensive and rare for common warriors)
Padded or leather garments (likely worn, but less archaeological evidence)

tools.description: Wide variety of tools for agriculture, crafts, shipbuilding, and daily tasks.
types: Farming implements (plows, sickles, scythes, hoes, spades)
Woodworking tools (axes, adzes, chisels, saws, augers)
Textile tools (spindle whorls, loom weights, needles, combs)

household_items.description: Items used in daily life within the home.
types: Keys and locks (evidence of securing goods)

transportation.description: Essential for travel, trade, raiding, and warfare.
types: Longships (langskip - fast, shallow-draft warships for raiding and exploration, sail and oar powered)
Knarrs (knǫrr - broader, deeper cargo ships, primarily sail powered, for trade and colonization)
Smaller boats (færingr - rowing boats for local transport and fishing)
Carts and Wagons (ox or horse-drawn for local transport)

styles.description: Distinctive animal styles evolving over time.

types.name: Borre Style
types.characteristics: Ring chain motif, gripping beasts with ribbon-like bodies and triangular heads, symmetrical compositions.

types.name: Jelling Style
types.characteristics: Single animal (often serpentine or bird-like) intertwined, s-shaped body, spiral hips, profile heads.

types.name: Mammen Style
types.characteristics: More substantial animal bodies, often single or paired, foliate elements, tendrils, axe heads are key examples.

types.name: Ringerike Style
types.characteristics: More defined animal forms (lions, birds, band animals), scrolled leaf motifs, runic inscriptions often integrated.

types.name: Urnes Style
types.characteristics: Elegant, elongated, asymmetrical animals (serpents, felines) with large almond-shaped eyes, fine lines, looping forms.

common_motifs: Gripping beasts (animals grasping themselves or borders)

materials: Metalwork (bronze casting, silverwork, goldwork, filigree, granulation, inlay)

culturally_significant_imagery: Mythological creatures (dragons, serpents, wolves - often linked to gods/myths)
Specific animals (ravens of Odin, horses of the gods)
Valknut (symbol with unclear specific meaning but associated with Odin and death/battle)
Representations of gods or mythological scenes (rare and debated)

natural_colors: Natural wool colors (white, grey, brown, black)

dyes_pigments.description: Colors derived primarily from plants and minerals.
sources: Madder (Rubia tinctorum) for red, pink, orange
Alder bark, walnut hulls, barks/roots (various browns, blacks)
Lichens (some species yield purples or reds)
Mineral pigments (ochre for red/yellow, charcoal/soot for black)
methods: Dyeing wool, linen, hemp fibers or finished cloth

status_color_associations.description: Brighter, more vibrant, and rarer colors were associated with higher status.
associations: Bright reds, clear blues, vibrant yellows (required mordants and skill, expensive dyes)
Purple (very rare and expensive, likely imported)
Natural or muted colors (more common, lower cost)

social_classes.description: Hierarchical society based on birth, wealth, and achievement.
classes: Jarls (Earls/Nobles): Highest class below the king, wealthy landowners, chieftains, advisors.
Karls (Free Farmers/Bondi): Independent landowners, backbone of society, warriors, could participate in Things.
Thralls (Slaves): Captured in raids or born into slavery, no rights, performed labor for Karls and Jarls. Could potentially buy freedom.

gender_roles.description: Defined roles but women had significant legal rights and authority within the household.
male_roles: Warriors, farmers, traders, craftsmen, explorers, chieftains, kings.
female_roles: Managed the household and finances (konan á fénu - 'the woman holds the wealth'), responsible for domestic crafts (weaving, cooking, brewing), could own property, inherit wealth, initiate divorce, held significant social influence within the family and community. Not typically warriors (though some sagas mention shield-maidens, historical evidence is debated).

family_structure.description: Extended family and kinship (ætt) were crucial for identity, protection, and alliances. Household (heimili) included family, thralls, and farmhands.
key_features: Patrilineal descent was important
Marriages were often strategic alliances
Blood feuds (víg) were a recognized mechanism for resolving disputes and maintaining honor, involving the wider kinship group

leadership.description: Leadership was often based on a combination of lineage, wealth, military prowess, success in raiding/trading, and ability to attract followers.
types: Konungr (King): Ruled kingdoms (size varied), power could be hereditary or contested.
Jarl (Earl): Powerful regional chieftains, often semi-autonomous or rivals to kings.
Goði (Chieftain/Priest in Iceland): Combined religious, political, and judicial authority (primarily in Iceland).
Herskír (War Leader): Leader of a raiding party or army.

daily_routines.description: Routines varied with the seasons and occupations, centered around farming and resource gathering.
typical_day: Tasks included tending livestock, working fields, crafting, fishing, preparing food, repairing tools and buildings
Evenings spent around the hearth, eating, storytelling, crafting

food_diet.description: Diet based on agriculture, animal husbandry, fishing, and gathering.
staples: Grains (barley, rye, oats) used for bread, porridge, and brewing ale
Meat (pork, beef, lamb, goat, fowl, game - often preserved by salting, smoking, drying)
Fish (freshwater and sea fish, often dried or smoked)

occupations.description: Majority were farmers, but specialization existed.
types: Craftsmen (smiths, woodworkers, shipwrights, jewelers, weavers, leatherworkers)

family_childrearing.description: Family was the core social unit. Children were integrated into household tasks from a young age. Naming was important.
practices: Children were named in a ceremony involving the father placing the child on his knee (signifying acceptance)
Infanticide of unwanted or deformed babies sometimes occurred, but was regulated
Children were educated through practical tasks, storytelling, and learning traditions
Fosterage (fostering children with other families, often for alliances or education) was common among elites

religious_spiritual.description: Worship of the Norse pantheon (Æsir and Vanir), focused on maintaining cosmic order and seeking favor for success and prosperity.
practices: Blót (Sacrificial rituals, typically involving animals, feasting, and consuming sacrificed meat and drink)
Sumbel (Ritualized drinking ceremony involving toasts, boasting, and oath-taking)
Offerings (gifts to gods at shrines, natural sites)
Seidr (Form of Norse magic or sorcery, often associated with prophecy and shamanic practices)

life_cycle_customs.birth: Child naming ceremony (ausu barni vatni - sprinkling with water, naming) where father acknowledges the child.
life_cycle_customs.coming_of_age: No specific widespread ceremony documented, transition marked by ability to perform adult tasks, participation in warfare/assemblies.
life_cycle_customs.marriage: Legal contract between two families, involving negotiation (máli) and exchange of property (dowry from bride's family, gift from groom). Ceremony involved feasting and symbolic acts.
life_cycle_customs.death: Funerary practices varied: inhumation (burial) or cremation. Grave goods were common, reflecting status and belief in afterlife needs (weapons, tools, jewelry, food, sometimes ships, horses, thralls). Elaborate mounds or stone settings marked graves.

seasonal_celebrations.description: Celebrations tied to the agricultural year and solar cycles.
celebrations: Yule (Jól - Winter Solstice festival, feasting, sacrifice, celebrating return of the sun, honoring gods like Odin and Freyr)
Sumarblót (Spring/Summer sacrifice, potentially linked to fertility and good harvest/raiding season)

important_ceremonies: Thing assemblies (Althing in Iceland, local/regional assemblies elsewhere - legal, political, social gatherings with ritual elements)
Feasts (central to social bonding, alliance building, and celebrating successes)

games_sports.description: Physical contests and board games were popular.
types: Hnefatafl (board game, 'Viking chess', strategic capture game)

music_instruments.description: Music was part of ceremonies, feasting, and storytelling.
instruments: Horn (animal horns used as trumpets or drinking vessels)
Possibly early forms of bagpipes or other wind instruments (less evidence)

storytelling.description: Oral tradition was central, preserving history, mythology, and heroic tales.
traditions: Sagas (prose narratives of historical events, family histories, voyages)
Skaldic Poetry (complex court poetry, often praising chieftains/kings, using elaborate metaphors - kennings)

behavioral_expectations.description: Emphasis on honor, bravery, self-reliance, and loyalty.
expectations: Courage in battle and facing adversity
Self-control and restraint (though outbursts of anger were common in sagas)
Respect for elders and those of higher status

taboos_forbidden.description: Actions considered shameful or harmful to the social order.
taboos: Oath-breaking (seen as a grave offense, undermining trust)
Refusing hospitality to travelers (a sacred duty)
Being accused of argr (unmanly or effeminate behavior, a severe insult for men)

honor_shame.description: Honor (æra) was paramount, acquired through brave deeds, wealth, reputation, and adherence to social codes. Shame (níð) was the loss of honor, a social death.
concepts: Drengrskapr (ideal conduct for a man: honorable, brave, generous, skilled)
Vígliga ('worth fighting over') - concept of value and honor
Seeking vengeance (víg) for insults or injuries to restore honor

hospitality_customs.description: A strong code of hospitality was expected, vital in a society with challenging travel.
customs: Hosts were expected to provide food, drink, and shelter to travelers
Guests were expected to behave respectfully and not overstay their welcome

common_expressions.meaning: What do you say? / How are you?

formal_speech.description: Formal settings, like the Thing or addressing a chieftain/king, likely involved more elevated language, adherence to protocol.

patterns: Given name followed by a patronymic (son of father's name) or less commonly a matronymic (daughter of mother's name). E.g., Björn Ragnarsson (Björn, son of Ragnar), Freydís Eiríksdóttir (Freydís, daughter of Eirík).
Often included nicknames (viðrnefni) describing a characteristic or deed.
common_elements: Often incorporated names of gods (Þór- / Tor-, Ás- / Ánz-)
Animal names (-ulfr/úlfr - wolf, -björn - bear, Hrafn - raven)
Elements related to battle/weapons (-víg, -geirr - spear, -hildr - battle)

patterns: Often descriptive of the geography (e.g., fjörðr - fjord, berg - mountain, dalr - valley, nes - headland)
Often combined a personal name or descriptive element with a settlement type (e.g., -býr - farm/settlement, -þorp - secondary settlement, -staðir - place, -land - land)
Many place names in areas conquered by Vikings (like the Danelaw) retain Norse origins (e.g., ending in -by, -thorpe)

title_systems.description: Titles indicated social status and role.

meaning_of_names.description: Names were often meaningful, invoking strength, divine protection, or desirable qualities.

language_structure.formal_vs_informal: Informal speech used among family and peers. Formal speech used when addressing superiors, in legal settings (Thing), or ceremonial contexts. Sagas show relatively direct speech, but formal contexts could involve more elaborate or stylized language.
language_structure.status_indicators_language: Using proper titles, displaying knowledge of genealogy and law, ability to compose or recite poetry could indicate status. Swearing oaths by powerful gods was a sign of seriousness.

poetic_specialized_language.description: Highly developed poetic language with complex rules.
forms: Eddic Poetry: Simpler verse forms, meter focused on stress and alliteration.
Skaldic Poetry: Complex meters (e.g., dróttkvætt), internal rhyme, strict rules, use of kennings and heiti.
poetic_specialized_language.kennings: Compound metaphors (e.g., 'whale-road' for sea, 'bone-house' for body, 'Odin's fire' for poetry).

language_structure.common_metaphors: Beyond kennings, common metaphors drawn from nature (sea, weather, animals), warfare, feasting, and mythology.

alphabets_scripts.description: Runes were the primary writing system used for inscriptions. Latin script began to appear later in the period with Christian influence.
scripts: Younger Futhark: The main runic alphabet in use during the Viking Age (16 staves).
Elder Futhark: Older, less common in this period (24 staves).

common_inscriptions.description: Runes were used for short inscriptions, not extensive texts.
types: Memorial stones (rune stones) commemorating the dead, their deeds, travels, or faith.
Possession markers (on tools, weapons, jewelry, combs).
Short messages or letters (on wood or bone).

literacy.description: Literacy was not widespread in the modern sense. Knowledge of runes was likely limited to a smaller group.
literacy.who_could_write: Runemasters (Rúnaristar) were skilled carvers. Others might have basic knowledge for simple marks. Literacy was not tied to social class exclusively; warriors, merchants, and farmers are known to have used runes.

terrain_features: Deep Fjords carving into the coastline
geography.settlement_patterns: Settlements were typically located near the coast, fjords, lakes, or rivers for access to water transport and resources. Inland settlements were often in valleys with access to arable land. Villages varied in size; scattered farmsteads were common. Trading towns (Kaupangr) were located at strategic coastal or riverine points.
important_locations: Coastal areas of Denmark and Southern Sweden (flatter, more agricultural)
natural_resources: Iron ore (found in bogs or mines)

seasonal_variations.description: Distinct seasons with significant variation in temperature and daylight.
seasonal_variations.winter: Long, cold, and dark winters, especially in the north. Heavy snow and ice cover common.
seasonal_variations.spring: Rapid thaw, increased water flow, preparation for farming.
seasonal_variations.summer: Short, mild summers with long daylight hours (midnight sun in the far north). Key period for farming, raiding, trading, and travel.
seasonal_variations.autumn: Harvest season, preparation for winter, shorter days, changing weather.

climate_challenges: Navigating frozen waters or rough seas
climate.weather_related_beliefs: Weather was often seen as influenced by gods (e.g., Thor controlling thunder and lightning, Njörðr controlling sea and wind). Appeasing gods was important for good weather and safe travel/harvests.

wild: Pine, Spruce, Birch, Oak, Ash, Elm

domestic_animals: Horses (smaller breeds, valued for riding and status)
wild_animals: Numerous Bird Species (eagles, ravens, falcons, waterfowl)

lighting_conditions.natural_daylight: Dramatic seasonal variation. Long daylight hours in summer (up to 24 hours north of Arctic Circle) and very short days in winter (minimal or no daylight north of Arctic Circle). Twilight is long.
artificial_lighting: Open hearth fires (primary light source in longhouses)
Oil lamps (using fish oil or seal blubber)
lighting_conditions.light_related_practices: Daily routines heavily dictated by natural light availability. Feasting and indoor activities were common during the long, dark winters.
lighting_conditions.visual_atmosphere: Often smoky and dim indoors from hearth fires. Dramatic contrasts between bright summer sun and long winter darkness. Natural light filtered through roof vents or doorways.

natural_sounds: Creaking of ice and snow in winter
human_activity_sounds: Sounds of weaving looms and other crafts
Sounds of ships (creaking timbers, splashing water, sails flapping)
Weapon sounds (clashing in practice or battle)
music_ceremonial_sounds: Chanting or ceremonial singing (for rituals, sagas, poetry recitation)
soundscape.silence_noise: Periods of relative silence, especially in winter or rural areas away from settlements/workshops. Trading towns and assembly sites (Things) were likely noisy and bustling. Sound carried differently depending on weather and landscape (e.g., echo in fjords).
